title: Static Routing
summary: Configuring static routes with next-hops and exit-interfaces, default gateways for end hosts, and default routes on Cisco routers.

sections.title: Review: the limits of connected and local routes

content.body:
Connected and local routes let a router reach its **own addresses** and **directly connected networks** — but nothing else. A router receiving a packet for a **remote network** (one not directly connected) has no matching route and must drop it.

For example, R1 with interfaces on 192.168.1.0/24, 192.168.12.0/24, and 192.168.13.0/24 cannot reach 192.168.4.0/24 (PC4's network).

**Static routes** solve this: manually configured routes that tell a router how to reach remote destinations.

End hosts can send directly to destinations on their **own** network. For anything outside it, they send the packet to their **default gateway** (an old term for router).

A host's default gateway configuration is a **default route**: a route to **`0.0.0.0/0`**. With a /0 mask, *no* bits are fixed, so it matches **every** IP address (over 4 billion). It is the **least specific** route possible, used only when no more-specific route matches. (A /32 route is the most specific, matching a single address.)

So a default route says: *"if nothing more specific matches, don't drop it — send it this way instead."* End hosts usually need nothing more than this.

sections.title: R1 has no route to PC4

steps.narration: PC1 (192.168.1.10) wants to reach PC4 (192.168.4.10), which is in a different network, so it sends the packet to its default gateway, R1.
R1 de-encapsulates the frame and checks its routing table. It has only connected and local routes — none match 192.168.4.10.
With no matching route, R1 drops the packet. R1 needs a static route to 192.168.4.0/24.

content.body:
A static route tells the router which **next-hop** to use for a destination network:

```
R1(config)# ip route 192.168.4.0 255.255.255.0 192.168.13.3
```

Format: `ip route <destination network> <netmask> <next-hop IP>`.

The route appears in the routing table with code **S** and the next-hop:

```
S   192.168.4.0/24 [1/0] via 192.168.13.3
```

The `[1/0]` are the route's **administrative distance** and **metric** — concepts covered later.

Remember, the CLI needs the **netmask in dotted decimal**, not slash notation.

For PC1 and PC4 to communicate, **every router in the path needs a route to both networks** — otherwise traffic can go one way but the replies get dropped. This is **two-way reachability**.

Using the path PC1 → R1 → R3 → R4 → PC4:

| Router | Needs a route to | Next-hop |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | 192.168.4.0/24 | 192.168.13.3 (R3) |
| R3 | 192.168.1.0/24 | 192.168.13.1 (R1) |
| R3 | 192.168.4.0/24 | 192.168.34.4 (R4) |
| R4 | 192.168.1.0/24 | 192.168.34.3 (R3) |

R1 already has a connected route to 1.0/24 and R4 to 4.0/24, so only the red routes must be added.

A router doesn't need routes to *every* network in the path — R1 only needs to know "send 4.0/24 traffic to R3; R3 will handle the rest."

There are three ways to write a static route:

1. **Next-hop only** — `ip route 192.168.4.0 255.255.255.0 192.168.13.3`
2. **Exit-interface only** — `ip route 192.168.1.0 255.255.255.0 g0/0`
3. **Both** — `ip route 192.168.4.0 255.255.255.0 g0/1 192.168.24.4`

With exit-interface only, the route shows the destination as "**directly connected**" even though it isn't, and forwarding relies on **proxy ARP** (beyond the CCNA scope). All three are valid; use whichever you prefer.

A **default route** is a static route to `0.0.0.0/0`:

```
R1(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.2
```

It's the **least specific** route, matching every destination, so it's used when nothing more specific matches — commonly to send all non-internal traffic toward the Internet.

In `show ip route`, the default route shows an **asterisk** (`S*`) marking it a *candidate default*, and the router reports the **"Gateway of last resort"**. Before a default route exists, that line says *"Gateway of last resort is not set"*.

sections.title: PC1 pings PC4 with static routes

steps.narration: PC1 sends the packet to its default gateway, R1. R1 looks up 192.168.4.10 and finds the static route via 192.168.13.3 (R3).
R1 forwards the packet to R3.
R3's route to 4.0/24 points to R4 (192.168.34.4), so it forwards the packet onward.
R4 has a connected route to 4.0/24, so it delivers the packet to PC4.
PC4 replies. The reverse path works because every router also has a route back to 192.168.1.0/24 — two-way reachability. The ping succeeds.

content.body: A **default route is `0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0`** plus a next-hop — the network *and* mask are both all zeros. It appears as `S*` and sets the *gateway of last resort*. When a static route is configured with only an exit-interface, the routing table shows the destination as "directly connected" even though it isn't.

questions.question: Which of the following commands configures a default route on a Cisco router?
questions.explanation: A default route uses 0.0.0.0 for both the network and the mask, and a next-hop IP. You must write the mask in dotted decimal (not slash notation), and the mask must be all zeros.

questions.question: R1's routing table has only a default route (next-hop 203.0.113.2) and a connected route to 203.0.113.0/24 on G0/2. Which interface will it use to forward packets destined for 8.8.8.8?
questions.explanation: 8.8.8.8 matches only the default route, whose next-hop is 203.0.113.2. That next-hop is on the directly-connected 203.0.113.0/24 network via G0/2, so R1 forwards out G0/2.

questions.question: R1 needs to reach PC4's network (192.168.4.0/24) via R2 at 192.168.12.2. Which command configures this static route?
questions.explanation: The format is `ip route <network> <mask> <next-hop>`. R2's address 192.168.12.2 is the next-hop toward 192.168.4.0/24.

questions.question: A route in R1's table shows code S and reads '172.20.0.0/16 is directly connected'. What command was used to configure it?
questions.explanation: The code S means it is a static route, not a connected (C) route. When you configure a static route with only an exit-interface, it appears as 'directly connected'. So the command was `ip route 172.20.0.0 255.255.0.0 g0/1`.

questions.question: R3 has connected routes to 192.168.13.0/24 and 192.168.34.0/24. How many static routes must it have to know ALL destination networks in the four-router topology (1.0/24, 4.0/24, 12.0/24, 24.0/24, 13.0/24, 34.0/24)?
questions.explanation: R3 already knows its connected networks (13.0/24 and 34.0/24). It needs routes to the four remaining networks: 192.168.1.0/24, 192.168.4.0/24, 192.168.12.0/24, and 192.168.24.0/24 — four static routes.
